17.1.simple: Arjuna asks about people who practise their faith sincerely but without following scripture: is their faith marked by clarity, restlessness or dullness? It is an honest question about sincerity versus guidance.

17.2.simple: Krishna answers that faith comes in three kinds, shaped by a person's nature: sattvic (clear and calm), rajasic (restless and driven) and tamasic (dull and confused).

17.3.simple: Everyone trusts in something, and that trust follows their inner nature. What you deeply believe and value shapes who you become; in a real sense, you are your faith.

17.4.simple: What people worship reveals their faith. Clear-minded people turn to the divine, restless people to powers of wealth and might, and dull-minded people to ghosts and spirits. Our devotions show what we truly value.

17.5.simple: Krishna describes people who perform harsh, extreme austerities that scripture never asked for, driven by show, ego, desire and attachment. Intensity alone is not the same as spiritual depth.

17.6.simple: Such extreme practices senselessly torment the body and even the Divine who lives within it. Krishna is clear: punishing yourself is not holiness.

17.7.simple: Krishna says food, offerings, self-discipline and giving each come in three kinds as well. Even everyday choices like what we eat reflect and shape our inner state.

17.8.simple: Food that is fresh, wholesome, nourishing and pleasant supports long life, clarity, strength, health and cheerfulness. Clear-minded people naturally enjoy food that truly nourishes.

17.9.simple: Food that is overly bitter, sour, salty, hot, pungent, dry or burning appeals to restless natures, but it brings discomfort, distress and illness. What excites the tongue may not serve the body.

17.10.simple: Stale, tasteless, spoiled, leftover or unclean food appeals to a dull state of mind. Neglect in how we eat mirrors and deepens a heaviness within.

17.11.simple: An offering or good deed is pure when it is done because it is right, without wanting a reward, steadily and with faith. A clean motive makes a clean act.

17.12.simple: When a good deed is done for a reward or to show off, it comes from restlessness. The same action with a different heart becomes a different thing.

17.13.simple: Rituals done carelessly, against guidance, without sharing food, without sincere words, gifts or faith, come from dullness. Going through the motions empties an act of its meaning.

17.14.simple: Discipline of the body means honoring the divine, teachers, elders and the wise, and practising cleanliness, straightforwardness, self-restraint and non-harming. Spirituality shows in how we carry ourselves.

17.15.simple: Discipline of speech means words that are true, kind and helpful and that do not stir others up, along with regular study of sacred texts. Speaking well is a real spiritual practice.

17.16.simple: Discipline of the mind means calm, kindness, quiet, self-control and pure intentions. Inner work counts just as much as outer effort.

17.17.simple: When these disciplines of body, speech and mind are practised with deep faith and no hunger for reward, they are sattvic: clear and pure.

17.18.simple: Discipline practised to win praise, honor or admiration, or as a show, comes from restlessness, and its results are shaky and short-lived. Effort made for applause fades with the applause.

17.19.simple: Discipline done out of confused thinking, through self-torture, or to harm someone else, comes from dullness. Self-control should never become self-harm or a weapon.

17.20.simple: A gift is pure when it is given simply because giving is right, at a fitting time and place, to someone worthy or in need, expecting nothing back.

17.21.simple: Giving in order to get something back, to earn a reward, or giving grudgingly, comes from restlessness. The hand gives, but the heart is still bargaining.

17.22.simple: Giving at the wrong time or place, to the wrong person, or with disrespect and contempt, comes from dullness. How we give matters as much as what we give.

17.23.simple: 'Om Tat Sat' are three sacred words that point to Brahman, the ultimate Reality. From that Reality came the wise, the sacred texts and acts of offering long ago.

17.24.simple: That is why followers of the sacred path begin their offerings, gifts and disciplines by saying 'Om.' It is a way of starting any act by remembering something higher.

17.25.simple: Seekers of freedom say 'Tat' ('That') as they offer, give and practise without seeking the fruits. It reminds them the act is not about what they will get.

17.26.simple: 'Sat' means what is real and what is good, and it is also used for any noble, auspicious act. Truth and goodness share one word.

17.27.simple: Steadiness in offering, discipline and giving is also called 'Sat,' and so is any action done for the sake of the Divine. Sincere, faithful effort is itself something real.

17.28.simple: Whatever is offered, given or practised without faith is called 'asat': hollow and unreal, bringing no benefit now or later. Sincerity is what gives our actions life.

lessons.title: You become what you trust
lessons.teaching: Everyone lives by some kind of faith, a deep trust in what matters most. Krishna says this faith follows your inner nature and, in turn, shapes who you become. Real faith is sincere, not showy or extreme.
lessons.keyIdea: As your faith is, so you become.

apply.scenario: A friend has started a punishing fasting and training routine, mostly to post dramatic progress photos online, and keeps urging you to join.
apply.question: What would the Gita suggest?
options: Join in; the more extreme the routine, the more it proves your commitment.
Ask what you truly value, and choose a sincere, healthy practice rooted in that.
Dismiss all self-discipline as ego; trying to improve yourself is pointless.
Secretly train even harder than your friend so you can prove you're better.
apply.why: In 17.3 Krishna says a person becomes what their faith is, and in 17.5 he points to harsh practices driven by show and ego. Sincere faith chooses what is truly good, not what looks impressive.

lessons.reflect: What do you trust most deeply right now, and how is that trust shaping who you are becoming?
lessons.practice: Write one thing you deeply believe in, and do one small act today that honors it.

lessons.title: Kind to the body within
lessons.teaching: Krishna says harming the body in the name of discipline is not holy, since the Divine dwells within it. Even food reflects our inner state: fresh, wholesome food brings health and cheerfulness, while harsh, extreme food brings discomfort. Caring for your body is part of the path.
lessons.keyIdea: Nourish the body that carries you; don't punish it.

apply.scenario: It's exam season and you're living on energy drinks, extra-spicy instant noodles and late-night junk food, and you feel jittery and run-down.
apply.question: What would the Gita suggest?
options: Push on as you are; health and comfort can wait until exams are over.
Skip meals entirely to save study time and toughen yourself up.
Add more caffeine and spicy snacks, since the kick keeps you alert.
Shift toward simple, fresh, nourishing meals that leave you steady and cheerful.
apply.why: In 17.8 Krishna says wholesome food increases life, strength, health and cheerfulness, while 17.9 says overly harsh food brings discomfort and illness. And 17.6 reminds us that tormenting the body is not true discipline.

lessons.reflect: How do you usually feel an hour after you eat: steady and light, or wired and heavy?
lessons.practice: Eat one fresh, simple meal slowly today, and notice how you feel afterward.

lessons.title: The heart behind the deed
lessons.teaching: The same good deed can be clear, restless or dull depending on why and how you do it. Done because it is right, without craving reward, it is pure; done for show, it is restless; done carelessly, it is empty. Krishna adds that bodily discipline is simple: cleanliness, honesty, respect and not harming others.
lessons.keyIdea: Do good because it is good, not because it is seen.

apply.scenario: Your company is organizing a volunteer day at a food bank, and you notice you mostly want to go so your manager sees you there.
apply.question: What would the Gita suggest?
options: Go, and let your motive shift: help because people need food, not to be noticed.
Skip it; if your motive isn't perfect, it's better not to help at all.
Go, and make sure to post photos so your effort gets proper credit.
Show up late, do the minimum, and leave once you've been counted.
apply.why: In 17.11 Krishna calls an offering pure when it is done as a duty without desire for reward, while 17.12 says acting for reward or show makes it restless. The answer is a cleaner motive, not doing nothing.

lessons.reflect: Think of something good you did recently. Would you still have done it if no one had ever known?
lessons.practice: Do one helpful thing today that no one will see or thank you for.

lessons.title: Gentle words, quiet mind
lessons.teaching: Krishna treats speech and thought as real spiritual practice. Words that are true, kind and helpful, and a mind that is calm, gentle and self-controlled, are a discipline as real as any fast. Practised sincerely, not for praise, they quietly transform a person.
lessons.keyIdea: True, kind and helpful: let your words pass all three.

apply.scenario: Your younger brother proudly plays you a song he wrote, and honestly, it still needs a lot of work.
apply.question: What would the Gita suggest?
options: Tell him it's perfect, since the truth would only hurt his feelings.
List every weakness bluntly; honesty matters more than feelings.
Share honestly what works and one thing to improve, warmly and encouragingly.
Say nothing and change the subject to avoid an awkward moment.
apply.why: In 17.15 Krishna describes disciplined speech as truthful, pleasant and beneficial, words that do not agitate. Honest and kind belong together, not one without the other.

lessons.reflect: Which is harder for you when you speak: being truthful, or being kind? Why do you think that is?
lessons.practice: Before speaking in one tense moment today, pause and ask: is it true, kind and helpful?

lessons.title: Giving with an open hand
lessons.teaching: Krishna says the purest giving happens because giving is right, at a fitting time, to someone in need, expecting nothing back. Giving to get something, giving grudgingly, or giving with contempt loses its goodness. He then names 'Om Tat Sat,' sacred words reminding us that good acts point toward something higher.
lessons.keyIdea: Give freely and respectfully, expecting nothing in return.

apply.scenario: A cousin going through a hard month asks to borrow some money. You can afford it, but you're tempted to attach conditions and remind them later.
apply.question: What would the Gita suggest?
options: Lend it, but make sure they know they now owe you a favor.
Give what you can afford, warmly and respectfully, without keeping score.
Hand it over along with a lecture about managing money better.
Refuse; people should always solve their own problems.
apply.why: In 17.20 Krishna calls a gift pure when it is given without expecting a return, at the right time, to someone who needs it. 17.21 and 17.22 note that grudging or disrespectful giving loses its goodness.

lessons.reflect: When you give, what do you quietly hope to get back: thanks, approval, or a feeling of being good?
lessons.practice: Give something small today, like time, help or a treat, and don't mention it afterward.

lessons.title: Sincerity makes it real
lessons.teaching: The sacred words Om Tat Sat are a way of beginning any act by remembering something greater and letting go of 'what's in it for me.' Krishna says steady, sincere goodness is itself 'Sat,' something real. What gives an action meaning is the faith and heart we bring to it.
lessons.keyIdea: Faith and sincerity are what make an action real.

apply.scenario: You've been helping care for your aging grandmother every weekend, and lately it feels like a mechanical chore you just tick off.
apply.question: What would the Gita suggest?
options: Stop going; if you don't feel it, it doesn't really count anyway.
Keep going through the motions; feelings don't matter if the task gets done.
Hand it off to a relative and step away until you feel motivated again.
Before each visit, pause to remember why you go, and offer the time with care.
apply.why: In 17.27 Krishna says steadiness in giving and acts done for a higher purpose are 'Sat,' real and good, while 17.28 says acts done without faith are hollow. Reconnecting with your reason brings the heart back.

lessons.reflect: Which everyday task might feel different if you began it by remembering why it matters?
lessons.practice: Before one routine task today, take a breath and silently dedicate it to something bigger than you.
